kind.instructions: state.code_head is the beginning (up to 1800 characters) of one inline <script> block printed inside the HTML of page state.page of a WordPress company website. state.script_id is the id attribute of the block and state.bytes is its full size. Decide what the script mainly does.

criteria.dom_patch_after_load: After the page loads, the script repairs or rewrites markup produced by the theme or plugins: it adds or changes aria attributes, roles, labels, tabindex, wraps or moves elements, or watches the DOM with MutationObserver to re-apply fixes.
criteria.fallback_for_deferred_js: The script re-implements or stubs behaviour of another script because that script is deferred, lazy-loaded or loads on first interaction, so that the first click still works.
criteria.feature: The script provides its own user-facing feature: a slider or carousel init, a language suggestion box, a scroll-to button, a table of contents, a reading progress bar, a form helper, a lightbox.
criteria.config_or_data: The script only holds data or configuration for another script: a JSON object, wp localize variables, JSON-LD structured data, a settings map.
criteria.third_party_tag: An analytics, pixel, tag manager, chat widget or ads snippet from a third party.
criteria.vendor_library: Minified library or framework code such as jQuery, Slick, Owl, Elementor runtime.
criteria.unknown: The code head does not show enough to decide.

belongs_in_file.instructions: state.code_head is the beginning of an inline <script> block of state.bytes bytes that is printed into the HTML of every page it applies to. Would an experienced WordPress developer ship this code as a separate enqueued .js file (cacheable, minified, versioned) instead of inline HTML? Answer yes when the block is larger than a few hundred bytes of real logic, is not a tiny config object, and is not a third-party tag that must stay inline.
